name: Rotating the List Values to the Right by Two Position
description: Construct a program that has a function that receives a list of values and returns the list rotated to the right by 2 position so that the value that is currently at the end of the list is moved to the second position, the second last value of the list is moved to the front of the list, and the remaining values are shifted to the right. For example, if the list is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], the program will change it to [5, 6, 1, 2, 3, 4].
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def rotate_right_by_2(lst):
    #Step 1.1: Store the last two values of the list in local variables
    last = lst[len(lst)-1]
    second_last = lst[len(lst)-2]
    #Step 1.2: Rotate the remaining values of the list to the right by 2 position
    for i in range(len(lst)-1, 1, -1):
        lst[i] = lst[i - 2]
    #Step 1.3: Move the last two values of the list to the front of the list
    lst[0] = second_last
    lst[1] = last
    return lst
#Step 2: Call the function
values = [3, 8, 9, 8, 7, 5]
print("Original list:", values)
print("Rotated list: ", rotate_right_by_2(values))

commentList: Purpose: This for-loop steps through the list indices from the last index down toward the front so you can move each element two places to the right without overwriting values you still need.

Syntax breakdown: range(len(lst)-1, 1, -1) produces indices starting at len(lst)-1 (the last index), stopping just after 2 (stop is exclusive), and stepping by -1, so i takes values len(lst)-1, len(lst)-2, ..., 2. The colon starts the loop block and the indented lines underneath run for each i.

Why it goes backward: You must move items from the end toward the front; if you moved from front to back you would overwrite elements that have not yet been copied. By decreasing i you preserve source values until you've copied them.

Common errors and misconceptions: A frequent off-by-one mistake is using the wrong stop value. If you used 0 as the stop, you would include index 1 and then copy into lst[1] incorrectly. Also using a forward range (e.g. range(len(lst))) will corrupt data because of overwriting.

Edge cases to watch: If the list is very short (length < 3) this loop either does nothing or can lead to unexpected behavior elsewhere. You should check the list length first (for example, return the list unchanged if len(lst) < 2) to avoid index errors or wrong results.

Best practice suggestion: For clarity and fewer index errors, consider using slicing: lst[:] = lst[-2:] + lst[:-2]. This expresses the intent directly and avoids manual index manipulation; keep the loop approach only if you want to practice in-place index work.

However, range's stop is not inclusive, so this will iterate i from len(lst)-1 down to 1. When i becomes 1 the assignment lst[i] = lst[i - 2] will use lst[-1] (because 1-2 = -1), which accesses the last element instead of a proper earlier element. That causes incorrect copying (you'll overwrite position 1 with the last element) and corrupts the list before you place the stored last-two values at the front. In short, this line wrongly allows i-2 to be negative, leading to unintended use of negative indices and an incorrect rotation rather than an error. It is plausible because of off-by-one thinking, but it fails to prevent negative indexing and so doesn't perform the intended shift.

Why you might pick this: you may remember that rotation involves copying nearby elements and mistakenly use the immediate neighbor (i-1) instead of two positions away. It looks simpler and feels like a small off-by-one tweak. What happens at runtime: this will shift every element only one position to the right instead of two. For example, with [1,2,3,4,5,6] the loop would produce a list equivalent to a 1-step rotation (like [6,1,2,3,4,5]) rather than the required arrangement. Why this is wrong for the task: the program must move items two places, not one, so using i-1 does not achieve the specified mapping of elements. Compared to the needed operation, this line is missing the step-size of two — it uses the wrong source index and therefore produces an incorrect final list even though it runs without error.
